period: Roman Egypt, late 1st century BC to 3rd century AD
summary: The most lifelike faces to survive from the ancient world: Egyptians with Greek names, painted in hot wax, looking at you from their mummies.
look: You may find this at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label. Thin wooden panels painted with a head and shoulders, turned slightly, eyes straight at you: large dark eyes, real hairstyles, earrings and necklaces, beards, children. Many panels have the top corners cut at an angle where they were fitted into the wrappings, and some are still bound into the mummy.
story:
When Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BC, its elite was a mix: descendants of the Greeks who came with the Ptolemies, Egyptians who had taken Greek or Latin names, soldiers and officials. They kept the Egyptian custom of mummification but added something Greek: a realistic portrait on a wooden panel, bound into the wrappings over the face. About 900 are known, most from the 1st to the 3rd century AD, from sites such as Hawara, er-Rubayat and Antinoopolis.

The finest are painted in encaustic, pigment mixed with hot beeswax; others in tempera with animal glue. The faces are so individual that they were long thought to have been painted from life and hung at home first; recent research is less sure. Hairstyles copied from the imperial court in Rome help to date them, such as the plaited styles of Trajan's time.

Flinders Petrie began digging at Hawara in 1887 and found 81 portrait mummies in his first season; only one or two percent of the mummies he excavated had portraits. Around the same time the Viennese dealer Theodor Graf acquired many from er-Rubayat. Their frontal gaze and big eyes strongly resemble later Christian icons, and some scholars see a direct link.
details: The eyes: enlarged and bright, with white highlights. The feature that makes them feel alive.
The paint surface: thick, ridged strokes of wax on the encaustic panels, smoother on tempera ones.
Hairstyles and jewellery: Roman fashions, used to date each portrait to within a few decades.
Gold leaf on some portraits: gilded wreaths or backgrounds.
The cut top corners of the panels: trimmed to fit into the mummy wrappings.
fun_fact: Encaustic comes from the Greek for 'burnt in'. These faces were painted with hot wax and have lasted about 2,000 years.
narration: If you have found them, these painted faces are the most lifelike portraits to survive from the ancient world, and they look straight back at you. They were made in Roman Egypt, mostly between the first and third centuries AD, on thin wooden panels, and bound into the mummy wrappings over the face of the dead. The sitters were the local elite, many with Greek names, some Egyptians who had taken Greek or Latin ones. Greek faces, Egyptian burial, Roman empire. The best are painted in encaustic, colour mixed with hot beeswax, a Greek word that means burnt in. Flinders Petrie found 81 portrait mummies at Hawara in the Fayum in his first season, starting in 1887, and noticed that only one or two mummies in a hundred had a portrait. Were they painted from life and hung at home first? People long thought so. Recent research is less sure. The hairstyles copy fashions from the imperial court in Rome, which is how they are dated. Look now at the eyes, enlarged and bright, and at the earrings and curls: real people from 2,000 years ago.

period: Mummies of the 17th to 20th Dynasties, c. 1560-1100 BC; moved 3 April 2021
summary: You will not find a single royal mummy at the Grand Egyptian Museum. In 2021 the kings and queens moved house, in a golden parade.
look: Nothing to look at here: this entry explains where the mummies went. The royal mummies of the New Kingdom, including Ramesses II, Seti I, Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Amenhotep III and Queen Tiye, are at the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization (NMEC) in Fustat, Old Cairo, in its Royal Mummies Hall. Tutankhamun stayed in his own tomb in Luxor.
story:
Most of these kings and queens reached Cairo through two ancient hiding places. In 1881 the royal cache at Deir el-Bahari, DB320, gave up dozens of royal mummies that priests had gathered and hidden about 3,000 years ago after waves of tomb robbery; in 1898 more were found in the tomb of Amenhotep II, KV35. For more than a century they lay in the Egyptian Museum on Tahrir Square.

On 3 April 2021, 22 of them, 18 kings and 4 queens, travelled about 5 km through Cairo to the NMEC. They rode in chronological order, from Seqenenre Tao, whose skull still shows axe wounds, to Ramesses IX, each on a gilded carriage, in containers filled with nitrogen. An orchestra played music by Hesham Nazih, the soprano Amira Selim sang ancient Egyptian hymns, and a 21-gun salute greeted the convoy. It was called the Pharaohs' Golden Parade.

Ramesses II had travelled before. In September 1976 his mummy flew to Paris to be treated against fungi and insects and was received at Le Bourget with full military honours. The popular story that he was issued a passport listing his occupation as 'King (deceased)' is a myth; the French word passeport was simply used for the paperwork. Under the microscope, his hair turned out to be naturally red.
details: NMEC is in Fustat, Old Cairo, beside the Ain el-Sira lake: a separate visit from the GEM.
At NMEC, Ramesses II: look for his hair, naturally red according to microscope studies.
Seqenenre Tao: the wounds in his skull suggest he died violently, probably in the war against the Hyksos.
Two more royal mummies, Ahmose I and probably Ramesses I, are in the Luxor Museum.
Tutankhamun is in KV62 in the Valley of the Kings, in a glass case in his own tomb.
fun_fact: Ramesses II has flown to Paris, been greeted with military honours, and ridden through Cairo in a gold carriage, all more than 3,000 years after his death.
narration: Here is a question many visitors ask in this building: where are the mummies? The answer is, not here. The royal mummies of the New Kingdom are at the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in Fustat, Old Cairo. On 3 April 2021, 22 of them, 18 kings and 4 queens, travelled about 5 kilometres from the old Egyptian Museum on Tahrir Square, in the Pharaohs' Golden Parade. They rode in chronological order, from Seqenenre Tao, whose skull still shows axe wounds, to Ramesses the Ninth, each on a gilded carriage, sealed in a container of nitrogen. Among them are Ramesses the Second, Seti the First, Hatshepsut, Thutmose the Third, Amenhotep the Third and Queen Tiye. Tutankhamun is the exception: he still lies in his tomb in Luxor. Ramesses had travelled before. In 1976 he flew to Paris for treatment against fungi and insects and was met with military honours. The famous story that he got a passport listing his job as king, deceased, is a myth. When you visit, look at his hair: microscopes showed it was naturally red.
